content: There are two primary strategies to prevent upper genital tract infections following a first-trimester abortion. The first involves administering antibiotics to all women around the time of the procedure. The second strategy, known as screen-and-treat, involves screening all women seeking an abortion for genital infections and treating only those who test positive. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of antibiotic prophylaxis in preventing post-abortal upper genital tract infections, identify the most effective antibiotic regimen, and determine the most effective prevention strategy. To achieve this, researchers conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving women undergoing either surgical or medical abortion during the first trimester. The trials compared various antibiotic regimens to placebo, no treatment, or other antibiotics, as well as the screen-and-treat strategy versus universal antibiotic prophylaxis. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), PubMed, EMBASE, POPLINE, and LILACS, with the last search conducted in May 2011. A total of 703 unique studies were identified, and 19 RCTs were included in the analysis. Two independent reviewers selected the studies and extracted data. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated, and meta-analyses were performed when appropriate. Heterogeneity between trials was assessed using the I² statistic, and 95% prediction intervals (PI) were estimated when heterogeneity was present. The analysis of 15 placebo-controlled RCTs demonstrated that antibiotic prophylaxis significantly reduced the risk of post-abortal upper genital tract infections. The pooled risk ratio was 0.59 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.75), indicating a 41% reduction in risk. However, the prediction interval (95% PI 0.30 to 1.14) and moderate heterogeneity (I² = 39%) suggested that the effectiveness of antibiotic prophylaxis might vary across different settings, populations, or interventions. There was insufficient data from three trials to determine whether one antibiotic regimen was superior to another. In one trial comparing the screen-and-treat strategy to universal antibiotic prophylaxis, the incidence of post-abortal upper genital tract infections was higher in the screen-and-treat group. The risk ratio was 1.53 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.36), suggesting a potential increased risk, although the confidence interval included the possibility of no difference. The authors concluded that administering antibiotic prophylaxis at the time of a first-trimester surgical abortion is effective in reducing the risk of post-abortal upper genital tract infections. However, the observed heterogeneity between trials indicates that this effect may not be consistent across all settings, populations, or interventions. The review did not identify the most effective antibiotic regimen, and the choice of antibiotics should consider the local epidemiology of genital tract infections, including sexually transmitted infections. Further RCTs comparing different antibiotics or combinations of antibiotics are needed, particularly in lowand middle-income countries and in populations with a high prevalence of genital tract infections among women seeking abortion.
